entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Novatian (died 258 CE) was a prominent Roman theologian, presbyter, and schismatic leader of the 3rd century, whose rigorous stance on readmitting lapsed Christians (lapsi) after the Decian persecution fundamentally challenged the burgeoning authority of the Roman bishopric and shaped early Christian penitential discipline. His election as a rival bishop of Rome in 251 CE, in opposition to Pope Cornelius, marked a critical moment in the development of the papacy and ecclesiastical unity, precipitating the Novatianist schism that persisted for centuries across the Roman Empire. This theological and political conflict illuminated deep divisions within the nascent Church regarding mercy, purity, and hierarchical power, with figures like Cyprian of Carthage playing a crucial role in opposing his views.

Following the intense Decian persecution (250-251 CE), which forced many Christians to apostatize, a fierce debate erupted over the conditions for their reintegration into the Church. Novatian, a highly educated and eloquent Roman presbyter, argued vehemently for a strict policy, contending that those who had sacrificed to Roman gods could not be absolved by the Church and readmitted to communion, but only by God himself at the Last Judgment. This unyielding position contrasted sharply with the more lenient approach advocated by Cornelius, who was elected Bishop of Rome in 251 CE. Believing Cornelius's policy compromised the Church's purity, Novatian was consecrated as a rival bishop by three Italian bishops, establishing a parallel hierarchy and initiating the Novatianist movement. This act led to his condemnation by a synod in Rome in 251 CE and subsequent excommunication.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Novatian's schism fundamentally challenged the emerging authority of the Roman See and forced the early Church to define its policies on forgiveness and ecclesiastical unity, influencing the development of penitential discipline for centuries. His actions led to a significant, long-lasting sectarian division.
